intro/hello: Welcome to localization, detection and segmentation.
intro/sofar: Every network so far has given one answer per image. This is a car. This is a cat.
intro/messy: Real pictures are messier. This street holds a car, two people, a dog and a cat.
intro/where: And usually we want to know where each one is, not just that it is in there somewhere.
intro/ladder: So this chapter climbs a ladder of harder tasks, each built from pieces you already have.
intro/cls: Classification gives one label for the whole image.
intro/loc: Localization adds a box around that one object: four more numbers.
intro/det: Detection finds a box and a label for every object, so the length of the answer changes from picture to picture.
intro/sem: Semantic segmentation labels every pixel. But two people standing together are just person pixels.
intro/inst: Instance segmentation gives each object its own mask, so the two people are finally told apart.
localize/one: Start with the gentlest step: one object we care about, and we want to find it.
localize/four: A box is four numbers: the left edge x, the top edge y, a width and a height.
localize/regress: Predicting real numbers is called regression. The last layer simply outputs four numbers instead of class scores.
localize/truth: To train it, compare with the true box, b star, drawn by a person. The prediction is b hat.
localize/err: Subtract, coordinate by coordinate: minus two, minus four, ten, minus five.
localize/square: Square each error, so misses in either direction count, and big misses count a lot.
localize/sum: Add them up: a hundred and forty five. A perfect box scores zero. This is the L2 loss.
localize/head: In practice, take a conv net trained to classify, and bolt on a second small head.
localize/both: One body, two heads. One answers what, with class scores. The other answers where, with four numbers.
localize/multi: Training adds the two losses: the softmax loss for the class, plus lambda times the box loss.
localize/lam: Lambda balances them. Too small, and boxes are sloppy. Too large, and classification suffers.
localize/specific: The head can predict one box for any class, or one box per class, so cats and buses each learn their own shape.
iou/how: Once a network outputs boxes, we need to grade them. How good is this purple box?
iou/want: We want one number: one for a perfect match, zero for no contact, and fair to boxes of every size.
iou/name: The standard answer is intersection over union, or eye oh you.
iou/inter: The intersection is the region inside both boxes, and it is itself a box.
iou/edges: Its left edge is the larger of the two left edges, and its right edge is the smaller of the two right edges.
iou/clamp: If the edges cross, there is no overlap, and that side is clamped to zero.
iou/union: The union is everything inside either box: both areas, minus the intersection, which was counted twice.
iou/ratio: Shared area over total area. That is eye oh you.
iou/shift: Slide a perfect box over by a quarter of its width, and eye oh you falls to zero point six.
iou/big: Make the box huge: it still covers the dog, but the union balloons, and the score collapses.
iou/tau: The usual rule: a detection is correct when its eye oh you with a true box is at least one half. We call that threshold tau.
sliding/one: To find objects anywhere, the obvious idea is to slide a window over the image, and ask the network about every crop.
sliding/each: A system called Overfeat did this, merging the good boxes at the end, and won ImageNet localization in 2013.
sliding/cost: The catch is cost. Every window is a full conv net forward pass.
sliding/count: Three sizes at a stride of thirty two is over three hundred passes. At a stride of eight, over four thousand, for one small image.
sliding/trick: The trick: a fully connected layer is just a convolution whose filter covers its whole input.
sliding/any: Rewrite every one, and the network is all convolutions, so it accepts an image of any size.
sliding/formula: Each layer's output size is input minus filter size, over the stride, plus one.
sliding/train: Built for fourteen by fourteen crops, our tiny network shrinks to ten, then five, then one cell of scores.
sliding/grow: Hand it sixteen by sixteen, and every layer keeps going, ending at two by two: four windows, scored at once.
sliding/share: Neighboring windows share most of their work, so this costs barely more than one pass.
nms/many: A detector that looks at many windows fires many times on one object: they all see the dog, so they all say dog.
nms/raw: Here are eighteen raw detections, as a detector might emit them.
nms/sort: Non-maximum suppression cleans this up. First, sort the boxes by score.
nms/keep: Keep the best one: the car, at zero point nine seven.
nms/drop: Then delete every box that overlaps it by more than a threshold tau, measured with eye oh you.
nms/repeat: Repeat with the best of what is left, until nothing is left.
nms/class: Only boxes of the same class compete, so a small cat box inside the dog's box survives.
nms/result: Eighteen in, eight out: one per object, a weak duplicate on the car, and two strays that a score cutoff would remove.
nms/tau: Tau is a tradeoff. Too high, and duplicates slip through. Too low, and you may delete a real object standing right beside another.
rcnn/vary: Why not regress boxes for detection too? Because the number of objects varies: one cat here, forty people there.
rcnn/clf: So treat detection as classification: look at many regions, and ask of each, which class is this, or is it background?
rcnn/props: Trying every position and shape is hopeless, so region proposals pick likely spots, using color, texture and edges.
rcnn/ss: Selective Search keeps merging similar neighboring patches, emitting a box at each merge: about two thousand, in a couple of seconds.
rcnn/recall: Proposals need not be precise, just high recall: nearly every object covered by at least one.
rcnn/rcnn: R C N N warps each proposal to the network's input size...
rcnn/feat: runs the conv net, scores the crop with a linear classifier per class, and refines its box with a regressor.
rcnn/deltas: That regressor predicts corrections to the proposal, called t, not raw pixel coordinates.
rcnn/txy: Move the center by t x proposal widths and t y proposal heights, so one regressor serves small and large boxes alike.
rcnn/twh: Stretch the width by a log ratio: zero keeps it, twice as wide is plus zero point six nine, and the width can never go negative.
rcnn/slow: A big jump in accuracy, but slow: two thousand conv net passes, about a minute per image.
fast/waste: Most of that work is wasted: overlapping proposals redo the same convolutions.
fast/once: Fast R C N N swaps the order. Run the convolutional layers once, on the whole image.
fast/proj: Then cut each proposal out of the feature map: divide by the stride, here forty pixels per cell.
fast/sizes: But regions come in all sizes, and the layers after them need a fixed size input.
fast/roi: Region of interest pooling splits the region into a fixed grid, here two by two...
fast/max: and keep the largest value in each cell, exactly like max pooling.
fast/any: Large region or small, the output is always two by two.
fast/e2e: Gradients flow through a max, so the whole network trains end to end: one loss for the class, one for the box.
fast/smooth: The box loss is smooth L1: a parabola near zero, a straight line beyond, so wild misses cannot dominate.
fast/fast: Training fell from eighty four hours to under ten. Testing, from forty seven seconds per image to a third of a second.
fast/bottle: Now the slowest part was the proposals themselves: two seconds per image.
faster/rpn: Faster R C N N lets the network propose its own regions.
faster/slide: A small region proposal network slides a three by three convolution over the shared feature map.
faster/anchor: At every position it considers k reference boxes, called anchors, centered on that spot.
faster/shapes: Three sizes times three aspect ratios: k is nine.
faster/obj: For each anchor it predicts an objectness score, and four offsets t, the same corrections as before.
faster/labels: In training, an anchor with eye oh you above zero point seven on a true box is a positive, below zero point three on all of them a negative, and the rest are ignored.
faster/fit: No single square fits a long car, a tall person and a small cat. Nine shapes fit every object better.
faster/best: Still, nothing here clears zero point seven, so each object's best anchor counts as positive too. The offsets do the fine work.
faster/pipe: The top boxes, after suppression, feed a Fast R C N N head on the same features: one network, four losses.
faster/speed: About a fifth of a second per image, at the same accuracy.
yolo/two: Faster R C N N still has two stages. yo-low, You Only Look Once, does it all in one pass.
yolo/grid: It cuts the image into an S by S grid: seven by seven.
yolo/resp: The cell that holds an object's center is responsible for detecting it.
yolo/boxes: Each cell predicts two boxes of five numbers: a center, a width and height, and a confidence that it holds an object and fits it.
yolo/classes: Each cell also predicts one set of class probabilities, shared by its boxes.
yolo/tensor: So the whole output is one block: seven by seven by thirty, for twenty classes.
yolo/score: A box's class score is its confidence times the class probability. Then threshold, and suppress.
yolo/fast: It ran at forty five frames per second, several times faster than Faster R C N N, though less accurate.
yolo/weak: Its weak spot is small objects in groups. On a three by three grid, the dog and cat share one cell, and one class guess.
yolo/ssd: S S D keeps the single pass, but predicts from several feature maps, so the finer maps catch small objects.
map/grade: How do we grade a whole detector? There is no fixed list of answers.
map/rank: Collect every detection on the test set, sort by score, and walk down the list.
map/tp: A detection is a true positive if it overlaps an unclaimed true box of its class with eye oh you of at least one half. Otherwise it is false.
map/cum: Keep running totals of both as you walk. That is cumsum.
map/prec: Precision asks: of the boxes we reported, what fraction were right?
map/rec: Recall asks: of the objects that exist, what fraction did we find?
map/trade: Walk further and recall rises, but more junk gets in, so precision tends to fall.
map/env: Smooth the curve into a staircase that never rises as recall grows.
map/ap: The area under it is the average precision: one for a perfect detector, zero point seven for this one.
map/mean: Average over every class for mean average precision, em ay pee: the headline number for detectors.
map/coco: COCO also averages over stricter eye oh you cutoffs, rewarding tighter boxes.
segment/pixel: Now the answer is a label for every pixel, and the training data is a label map the size of the image.
segment/loss: And the loss is one you know: the softmax loss, at every pixel, averaged.
segment/how: The hard part is a network whose output is a full resolution map.
segment/slow: Classifying a patch around every pixel works, but it is absurdly slow.
segment/down: The design that won: downsample cheaply, then upsample back to full size, inside the network.
segment/fcn: Fully convolutional networks made an ImageNet classifier all convolutions, and added learnable upsampling at the end.
segment/blob: But its last map has stride thirty two. Upsampled from there, the two people melt into one blob, and the cat loses its ears.
segment/skip: The fix is skip connections: add in scores from earlier, finer layers, at stride sixteen...
segment/eight: and stride eight. Each skip halves the cell size and recovers detail.
segment/what: Deep layers know what. Shallow layers know where. Together, they paint a sharp map.
upsample/grow: How does a network make a feature map bigger? Two families of layers do it.
upsample/near: Unpooling learns nothing. Nearest neighbor copies each value into a two by two block.
upsample/nails: Bed of nails puts each value in one corner, with zeros everywhere else.
upsample/max: Max unpooling puts each value back where the max sat during pooling.
upsample/tconv: The learnable option is the transpose convolution. A normal convolution reads a window to write one output.
upsample/rev: This does the reverse: it reads one input, scales the whole filter by it, and writes that block out.
upsample/stamp: Input three stamps three, six, three. Step two places, and input five stamps five, ten, five.
upsample/add: Where stamps overlap, they add: the middle gets three plus five. The output is three, six, eight, ten, five.
upsample/names: It is often called deconvolution, which misleads: it does not undo a convolution.
upsample/why: Transpose is exact. A stride two convolution is a matrix multiply, and this layer multiplies by its transpose, taking two numbers back up to five.
upsample/learn: It restores the shape, not the numbers, and its filter is learned like any other weights.
upsample/checker: In two dimensions the stamps overlap unevenly, which is why generated images can show faint checkerboards.
outro/inst: The top rung, instance segmentation, combines the two: find each object, then label its pixels.
outro/era: In 2016 that meant R C N N with a mask step bolted on.
outro/mask: A year later, Mask R C N N made it standard: Faster R C N N, plus a small head that paints a mask inside every box.
outro/recap: So, the ladder. Localization is regression: four more numbers beside the class.
outro/grade: eye oh you grades a box, suppression removes duplicates, and em ay pee grades a detector.
outro/det: Detection got practical with proposals, fast with shared convolutions, and faster with anchors. yo-low and S S D do it in one look.
outro/seg: And segmentation is classification at every pixel: down, then up, with skips for detail.
outro/next: Next, networks with memory: recurrent networks, which read and write sequences, and can describe a whole image in a sentence.
